The New Deal and World War II (1934–1945)

stimulus.source_note: Woodrow Wilson, Fourteen Points address to Congress, January 8, 1918, public domain.
stimulus.text: From President Woodrow Wilson’s Fourteen Points address to Congress, January 8, 1918: “What we demand in this war, therefore, is nothing peculiar to ourselves. It is that the world be made fit and safe to live in; and particularly that it be made safe for every peace-loving nation which, like our own, wishes to live its own life, determine its own institutions, be assured of justice and fair dealing by the other peoples of the world as against force and selfish aggression.”

source: original; stimulus verbatim public-domain text, Woodrow Wilson, Fourteen Points address to Congress, January 8, 1918, public domain.
stem: A historian comparing Wilson’s goals in this passage with the peace settlement the United States accepted after World War II would most reasonably argue that...

options.text: the United States abandoned Wilson’s ideals entirely and imposed a purely punitive peace on its enemies in 1945.
options.misconception: The 1945 settlement built the United Nations and rebuilt former enemies; it was not purely punitive.

options.text: the United States carried Wilson’s ideals further in 1945 by joining the United Nations and accepting lasting international commitments.
the United States repeated its 1919 refusal and stayed out of every postwar international organization.
options.misconception: The United States joined the United Nations in 1945, the opposite of repeating the 1919 refusal.

options.text: the United States made self-determination its only war aim in both wars and ignored economic rebuilding.
options.misconception: After 1945 the United States funded rebuilding through the Marshall Plan; economics was central, not ignored.

rationales.A: The 1945 settlement built the United Nations and rebuilt former enemies. It was not a purely punitive peace.
rationales.B: The ideals are the same: self-determination and collective security. Background: what changed was the American commitment. In 1945 the United States joined the United Nations as a founding member and kept alliances and troops abroad.
rationales.C: The United States joined the United Nations in 1945. That is the opposite of repeating the 1919 refusal.
rationales.D: After 1945 the United States funded rebuilding through the Marshall Plan. Economics was central to the settlement, not ignored.
rationales.general:
1. Pull out Wilson’s ideals. Self-determination for nations and safety through collective action.
2. Check 1945 against them. The United Nations Charter promises both, and America signed it.
3. Find the difference. In 1919 America stayed out; in 1945 it joined and stayed engaged.
4. Put it together. The ideals survived the failure of 1919, and the second try fixed the commitment, not the vision.
Remember: continuity and change can live in one answer. The idea stayed the same while the country’s willingness to act on it changed.
